title: SVK-1999-1-002 — Violation of fundamental right
text:
The constitutional right to have a case settled within a reasonable time is violated not only if the court deciding on the case is passive: the wrong kind of activity by the court can also cause a violation of that constitutional right.

An individual submitted to the Constitutional Court a petition claiming violation of the right guaranteed under Article 48.2 of the Constitution which, in the part relevant to the case, reads: "Every person has the right to have his or her case tried publicly without unreasonable delay".

This right was claimed to have been violated by the District Court at Dunajská Streda. On 2 January 1996 the petitioner applied to this court requesting that a person be designated to take care of a minor. The petitioner was the grandmother of the minor in question and asked the District Court to designate her as the child's guardian. The first hearing in the case took place on 28 February 1996. Seven more hearings took place between then and September 1998. The case, however, was never decided. The mother and the stepfather of the child are Canadian residents. From time to time, they visit Slovakia to settle cases relating to inheritance and restitution of their property. The District Court at Dunajská Streda made no attempt to address the Canadian authorities for their legal assistance. The District Court only addressed the Slovakian local self-government authority in the place where both visitors lived during their stay in Slovakia with various requests such as the visitors' address in Canada. The District Court fixed hearings on days when the mother of the child and her husband were in Canada. The District Court did not examine in time the motion to pass a preliminary decision preventing the mother from leaving Slovakia with the minor before being heard by the District Court. In short, the district Court took a number of steps in the case but they were seldom related to the decision on the merit of the case. This was the reason for the petition to the Constitutional Court.

When deciding on the right to have a case settled within a reasonable time, the Constitutional Court takes into account three criteria compatible with the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the conduct of the judicial authority. In this case, the last criterion was the most relevant. The Constitutional Court began by considering the purpose of the right to have a case settled within a reasonable time. The purpose of this right for the applicant is to be free from legal uncertainty in relation to the case. While this uncertainty exists, the purpose of the right to have the case settled is not fulfilled. It is irrelevant whether the uncertainty lasts owing to the inactivity of the judicial authority or to its carrying out the wrong kind of activity. Legally irrelevant acts made before the court, and even by the court, make no contribution to settling the merits of the case. Thus, if they occur and insufficient action is taken to rule on the merits of the case, the Constitutional Court ruled that the right to have a case settled within a reasonable time is violated.
